title: The Stinson Family Newsletter
logline: In 2005 Barney invented a wife, a son and a live-in mother to win a promotion, and kept them alive with a holiday newsletter nobody reads. When GNB makes Family Day mandatory, the gang plays the Missus, Junior, Grandma and an uninvited brother-in-law, only to find that everybody read the newsletter, and every story in it is about them.
coldOpen: Kids, in the fall of 2013, your Uncle Barney had a wife, a sixteen-year-old son, a terrifying mother and a brother-in-law who was an architect. For one afternoon, they were the happiest family at Goliath National Bank. None of them existed. Every one of them was real.

couch.line: Let me guess. Aunt Robin played the wife.
Penny, the casting was purely practical.

guests.name: Ruthanne Pilsbury
guests.role: GNB's Director of Human Resources, who ran Barney's promotion review in 2005; beaming and relentless, she meets every answer with 'Follow-up question!' and has waited eight years to meet the Stinson family

guests.name: Phil Draper
guests.role: a meek risk analyst in the office next to Barney's and a father of five, who has laminated every issue of the Stinson Family Newsletter and reads them aloud to his kids every Christmas Eve

scenes.summary: Barney arrives with the Family Day memo, which names him personally. Flashback to 2005: Ruthanne's promotion review, where Barney invents the Missus, Junior and Grandma on the spot. He has kept them alive with a holiday newsletter. Casting: Robin is the Missus (a bush pilot, her terms), Marshall is Junior (now sixteen, sold on the kids' sundae bar), Lily is Grandma (sold on the power), Ted invites himself as the brother-in-law to see the boardroom ceiling. Runner setup: Ted's twenty-five-minute doorway toast. Button: nobody reads a newsletter.

beats.line: It started with a memo.
Guys. Code red. GNB is having a Family Day.
So skip it. You don't have a family.
Attendance is mandatory. Read it.
Yes, Barney, this means you. They put you in the memo.
beats.title: GNB Family Day. Saturday. Attendance mandatory.
lines: Spouses, children and live-in relatives required.

beats.line: Why would your bank think you have a family?
Because I told them. In 2005, I was up for a promotion, and the board only promoted family men.
Mister Stinson, the board loves you. But the other finalist, Doug, has a wife and three kids.
Ruthanne, I'm a huge family man. Massive. Ask anyone in my family.
Ooh. Follow-up question. What's your wife's name?
The Missus.
Follow-up question. Children?
One son. Barney Junior. He's eight. He loves sports. All of them. Equally.
Follow-up question. Anyone else at home?
My mother. She lives with us. Because I'm a wonderful son.
Follow-up quest—
Ruthanne, I'd love to, but it's Junior's bath time.
So your family is the Missus, Junior and Grandma.
Simple names. Easy to remember. Impossible to trace.
Barney, lying to HR for a promotion is fraud.
Marshall, it's only fraud if they find out.
That is the exact opposite of how fraud works.
And nobody noticed in eight years?
I keep them alive. Every December, the whole floor gets the Stinson Family Newsletter. Fifteen hundred words. Mostly vague.
Which means by Saturday, I need a family. Robin. You're the Missus.
Pass.
Robin, you're the only woman I know who can lie under fire.
Fine. But I'm not playing some trophy wife who laughs at your jokes.
The Missus laughs at all my jokes.
Then the Missus has a head injury.
My Missus is a bush pilot from the Yukon. Cold. Distant. Never home.
Huh. That's surprisingly hot.
Marshall. You're Junior.
Your son? Barney, I'm six foot four. I own a juicer.
Wait. Junior was eight in 2005. That makes him sixteen.
I have a teenager.
Marshall. Kids under eighteen eat free at the sundae bar.
What time should I be ready, Dad?
And Grandma? You can't bring your actual mom?
Loretta? At my bank? She'd tell my boss how I was conceived. With a diagram.
Lily. You're Grandma.
I'm younger than you!
Grandma is tiny, terrifying and banned from two Pottery Barns. You're perfect.
That's weirdly specific.
Wait. If I'm your mother, you have to do what I say? In front of your boss?
Within reason.
Barney. Mothers don't have reason.
And me? Every family has a brother-in-law.
And your boardroom has an original 1931 coffered ceiling. I'll be the Missus's brother.
You'd fake being my brother to look at a ceiling.
It's coffered, Robin!
Fine. But no toasts.
I give beautiful toasts. At my cousin's wedding, I did twenty-five minutes on the church doorway.
Three people left. One of them was the groom.
Saturday. Nine a.m. Family up!
Barney, what if your coworkers ask about the newsletter?
Lily, please. Nobody reads a newsletter.
Everybody read the newsletter.

scenes.summary: Saturday, riding up to Family Day in costume (Ted went ahead for the ceiling). Barney's final check: Robin's bush pilot, Marshall's sullen teen who can't stay sullen, Lily already calling him Barnaby and grounding everyone. Phil from next door gets on: he has laminated every newsletter. Every follow-up question exposes an improvisation: skydiving church, Robin denouncing hockey, Marshall's Fiero, Marshall's twin in legal, Grandma's age. Button: Ruthanne has follow-up questions. To eight years.

beats.line: That Saturday, the Stinsons rode up to Family Day. Uncle Ted had gone ahead to see the ceiling. He'd been there since seven.
Final check. Missus. Backstory.
Bush pilot. Yukon. I don't talk about the crash.
Junior.
Sixteen. Sullen. Into video games.
Ugh. Whatever, Dad.
Sorry! That was so mean. I love you, Dad.
Grandma.
Barnaby, stand up straight.
My name is not Barnaby.
It is today.
Now hold still. You've got schmutz on your face. Mommy's got spit.
Mom!
She's enjoying this way too much.
She's been practicing on me since Thursday. I've been grounded four times.
Barney! Oh my gosh. Is this the family?
Phil. Risk analysis, next office over. Phil, the Stinsons.
I feel like I'm meeting celebrities. I've read every newsletter. Twice. I laminate them.
Nobody reads a newsletter?
Phil's a risk analyst. He reads the backs of shampoo bottles.
Missus, I've always wondered. How did you two meet?
Church.
Skydiving.
Skydiving church?
Very progressive congregation. Communion at twelve thousand feet.
And are you still a huge hockey fan? Thursday nights, section one twelve?
Hockey? Ugh. No. Too violent. I'm more of a figure skating person.
I just said ugh about hockey. I need a scotch and a priest.
And Junior! You're a lot bigger than I pictured.
I'm sixteen.
Kids, your Uncle Marshall was thirty-five. He had a mortgage, a bad knee and a favorite brand of fiber.
Sixteen! Do you still drive that old Fiero?
I love my Fiero!
Wait. How do you know about my Fie—
Junior loves all cars! Phil, how are your kids? Tell us everything about your kids.
You look so familiar. Did you ever work in legal, on nine?
No. That was my twin. We don't speak. He's a lawyer.
And Grandma! You look wonderful. How old are you?
Sixty-eight.
Wow! What's your secret?
Pilates and grudges. Mostly grudges.
Barney always says you're terrifying.
Aw, Barnaby. That's so sweet. You're still grounded.
My kids act out the newsletter every Christmas Eve. My youngest always fights to play Grandma.
Oh! Ruthanne from HR has been waiting all morning. She has follow-up questions.
Follow-up questions to what?
Eight years.

scenes.summary: Family Day in Barney's office. Ted's coffered ceiling is drywall; Marshall got reported at the sundae bar. Ruthanne arrives with follow-up questions: a hot air balloon over a prison. She knows Uncle Ted from the doorway toast (runner: it was twenty-five minutes). Phil brings the 2009 issue: every story in it is the gang's. Barney: you were just there, being weird. Lily grounds Barney and sends him to the corner. Barney confesses. Ruthanne and Phil have known since 2007: Family Day was mandatory so he'd finally bring them. Lily undercuts. Button: 'Follow-up question.' 'No!'

beats.line: The boardroom ceiling is drywall. Painted to look coffered. In 1998.
So it's fake.
It's a lie, Robin. A beautiful, symmetrical lie.
Ted, today we don't judge those.
The sundae bar is a scam. A seven-year-old called me sir. Then she called security.
Okay. I've got my character. Ted Scherbatsky. Your brother. From Canada, eh?
Say eh one more time and I'll make myself an only child.
The Stinsons! In my building! Finally!
Eight years I've asked to meet them. Follow-up question. Why eight years?
Scheduling.
Follow-up question. All eight years?
We're a very busy family.
Missus! How did you two meet?
Hot air balloon.
Prison.
Follow-up question. A hot air balloon over a prison?
It was a very romantic jailbreak.
And who's this?
Ted Scherbatsky. The Missus's brother. Architect.
Uncle Ted! From the newsletter! You gave the forty-minute toast about a doorway!
It was twenty-five minutes.
Wait. How does she know about my toast?
I brought the 2009 issue! Would the family sign it?
Junior cried at the end of a Bigfoot documentary. Then made us watch it again.
beats.title: The Stinson Family Newsletter. Holiday 2009.
lines: Junior cried at the end of a Bigfoot documentary. Then made us watch it again.
Grandma got banned from her second Pottery Barn.
Uncle Ted gave a forty-minute toast about a doorway.
The Missus made a New York Ranger cry. He had it coming.

beats.line: Because it's better the second time!
Wait. That was me. On your couch.
Banned from my second Pottery Barn. That's me!
And I made a Ranger cry at MacLaren's. He called the Canucks a farm team.
Barney. The newsletter is us.
You try making up a family from scratch! You guys were just there. Being weird. Every single day.
Follow-up question! Grandma, is it true you made a father cry at a parent-teacher conference?
Twice. And he knows what he did.
Mom, maybe let's not—
Don't you Mom me. You lied to this nice woman for eight years. You're grounded.
Follow-up question. Grounded from what?
Phone. Scotch. Saturdays. Corner, Barnaby. Now.
Lilypad, I think you're enjoying this too much.
Baby, I've never felt so alive.
Aunt Lily put Uncle Barney in time-out? At his job?
Luke, it was the most productive he'd ever been there.
Barney, come out of the corner. Last follow-up question.
Is any of this real?
No. No Missus. No Junior. No Grandma. I made them up for the promotion.
I know.
You know?
Barney, your son learned to ride a bike three times. In 2006, 2009 and 2011.
And Grandma got eight years younger every Christmas.
Then why make Family Day mandatory?
So you'd finally bring them.
Every December you write fifteen hundred words about four people you obviously can't live without. We just wanted to meet them.
Barney, are you crying?
He gets weepy when he skips his nap.
Ooh! Follow-up question—
No!

scenes.summary: Ranjit drives the Stinsons home. Lily refuses to stop being Barney's mother and has grounded Marshall pre-emptively. Ted learns that in issue four he built Junior a treehouse with flying buttresses. Ranjit asks the question everyone asked all day; Barney and Robin finally tell the true how-we-met. Robin asks if they would have been like the newsletter; Barney: better, the newsletter had a word limit. Lily grounds them both. Future Ted: the newsletter still goes out, and it was twenty-five minutes. Thirty, tops.

beats.line: Barnaby. Seatbelt.
Lily, it's over. You can stop being my mother.
I can't, Barney. I've tasted power.
She grounded me too. No Bigfoot until Tuesday. I didn't even do anything!
It's for something you're going to do.
Barney. Am I in the other issues?
Issue four. You build Junior a treehouse. It has flying buttresses.
It would need flying buttresses.
Hello! Mister Barney, Miss Robin. Everyone asked you today, so now I ask. How did you two meet?
Ranjit, we're not married.
I know. Tell me anyway.
She walked into MacLaren's with Ted. Ordered a scotch, neat. Didn't laugh at a single one of my jokes.
He was wearing a suit to a bar on a Tuesday. I thought, that guy is trouble.
And?
And I was right.
The Missus in your newsletter. She sounds happy.
She is. Eight years straight.
Would we have been like that? If we'd actually done it?
Better. The newsletter had a word limit.
Okay, that's enough. You're both grounded.
Kids, the Stinson Family Newsletter still goes out every December. I'm in every issue, giving that forty-minute toast about a doorway.
For the record, it was twenty-five minutes. Thirty, tops. It was a really good doorway.
